power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: We acknowledge the contribution of Dipl.-Statistikerin Nadine Bonberg, who assisted with the estimation of the sample size required for the study.
ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used to assist with language editing and to improve the readability of the manuscript.
All scientific content, interpretations, and conclusions were generated, reviewed, and verified entirely by the authors.
Long scan times and motion artifacts continue to limit MR performance in clinical practice.
Shorter acquisitions improve patient comfort, reduce motion artifacts, and enhance efficiency (1, 2).
text.formatted: Shorter acquisitions improve patient comfort, reduce motion artifacts, and enhance efficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2)</ref>.

text.text: With newer scanner generations, advanced acceleration techniques make this increasingly feasible in routine imaging (3, 4).
text.formatted: With newer scanner generations, advanced acceleration techniques make this increasingly feasible in routine imaging <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4)</ref>.

text.text: Parallel imaging (PI) techniques such as GRAPPA (Generalized Autocalibrating Partially Parallel Acquisition) and CAIPIRINHA (Controlled Aliasing in Parallel Imaging Results in Higher Acceleration) substantially shorten acquisition times across many MR sequences (5) (6) (7) (8) (9).
text.formatted: Parallel imaging (PI) techniques such as GRAPPA (Generalized Autocalibrating Partially Parallel Acquisition) and CAIPIRINHA (Controlled Aliasing in Parallel Imaging Results in Higher Acceleration) substantially shorten acquisition times across many MR sequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>.

text.text: More recently, compressed sensing (CS) has emerged as an additional acceleration method, exploiting the inherent sparsity of MR data, enabling undersampled acquisitions and reconstruction of full datasets for shorter scan times or higher spatial resolution (10).
text.formatted: More recently, compressed sensing (CS) has emerged as an additional acceleration method, exploiting the inherent sparsity of MR data, enabling undersampled acquisitions and reconstruction of full datasets for shorter scan times or higher spatial resolution <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: However, acceleration is constrained by potential image quality loss and reconstructionrelated artifacts (11) (12) (13) (14).
text.formatted: However, acceleration is constrained by potential image quality loss and reconstructionrelated artifacts <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: TOF-MRA is an established non-invasive technique for the detection and follow-up of intracranial aneurysms (15, 16).
text.formatted: TOF-MRA is an established non-invasive technique for the detection and follow-up of intracranial aneurysms <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16)</ref>.

text.text: Owing to its high spatial resolution and ability to visualize intracranial vessels without contrast administration or ionizing radiation, TOF-MRA is widely used for screening and surveillance, particularly in patients requiring repeated imaging.
The advantages of CS in TOF-MRA have been demonstrated in studies of extracranial and intracranial arterial pathologies, including stenoses and moyamoya disease (17) (18) (19).
text.formatted: The advantages of CS in TOF-MRA have been demonstrated in studies of extracranial and intracranial arterial pathologies, including stenoses and moyamoya disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: These studies showed that CS-based TOF-MRA reduces acquisition time while maintaining or improving image quality, vessel delineation, and artifact reduction compared with conventional TOF-MRA (20, 21). .
text.formatted: These studies showed that CS-based TOF-MRA reduces acquisition time while maintaining or improving image quality, vessel delineation, and artifact reduction compared with conventional TOF-MRA <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21)</ref>. .

text.text: In aneurysm-focused studies, mainly at 3T, CS-TOF has shown comparable or improved image quality versus PI-TOF, with fewer artifacts and equivalent aneurysm size measurements when validated against DSA (22).
text.formatted: In aneurysm-focused studies, mainly at 3T, CS-TOF has shown comparable or improved image quality versus PI-TOF, with fewer artifacts and equivalent aneurysm size measurements when validated against DSA <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref>.

text.text: To date, no studies have systematically compared CS-with conventional GRAPPAacceleration for intracranial aneurysm assessment using TOF-MRA on widely available 1.5T systems, as most prior work has focused on 3T.

In this prospective paired non-inferiority sequence-comparison study, we compared optimized CS-and GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T in clinical routine, using overall image quality as the primary endpoint and additional image quality assessments and interrater reproducibility of aneurysm diameter measurements as exploratory secondary endpoints.
This single-center prospective sequence-comparison study was approved by our institutional ethics committee of Carl von Ossietzky Universität Oldenburg, Germany (registration no.
Sample size was estimated based on a precursor pilot study with a retrospective analysis of routine clinical MRI data.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
No contrast agent or sedative medication was administered for study purposes.
However, patients who received contrast agents and/or sedation for clinical reasons were eligible.

During the first stage, sequence parameters for newer (CS) and conventional (GRAPPA) acceleration techniques were optimized in five healthy participants using a pragmatic empirical approach (see supplementary material).
Based on expert consensus, the bestperforming sequence from each acceleration arm was selected for the clinical phase (Table 1).
text.formatted: Based on expert consensus, the bestperforming sequence from each acceleration arm was selected for the clinical phase (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: During the second stage, the previously optimized CS-accelerated and GRAPPA-accelerated sequences were added to routine clinical MRI examinations of patients with at least one known untreated intracranial aneurysm, as indicated by neurological/neurosurgical referral information.
Both sequences were acquired natively, although the overall protocol might have included contrast administration.
The acquisition order of CS and GRAPPA was systematically alternated.
The subsequent comparison included an assessment of general and specific aspects of image quality as well as measurement of aneurysm diameters.

The primary endpoint was overall image quality, with the primary hypothesis that optimized CS-accelerated 3D-TOF would not result in a clinically relevant reduction in overall image quality (>10%) compared with GRAPPA-accelerated TOF.
text.formatted: The primary endpoint was overall image quality, with the primary hypothesis that optimized CS-accelerated 3D-TOF would not result in a clinically relevant reduction in overall image quality (>10%) compared with GRAPPA-accelerated TOF.

text.text: Secondary endpoints included comparison of general image artifacts (numerical rating scale), motion artifacts (numerical rating scale), CNR (numerical rating scale and ROI-based measurements), aneurysm delineation (numerical rating scale), overall aneurysm depiction (numerical rating scale) as well as aneurysm diameters.
During sequence optimization, 5 healthy volunteers (≥18 years) were recruited.
Based on the sample size estimation pilot study, the final cohort comprised 25  A CS acceleration factor of 7 was applied, resulting in a scan time of 3:04 min:s.
text.formatted: Based on the sample size estimation pilot study, the final cohort comprised <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref>  A CS acceleration factor of 7 was applied, resulting in a scan time of 3:04 min:s.

text.text: For GRAPPA-accelerated TOF, a GRAPPA factor of 2 was used, yielding a scan time of 5:00 min:s (38.7% scan time reduction).
Both 3D-TOF-MRA datasets were acquired in the axial plane.
Detailed imaging parameters are summarized in Table 1.
text.formatted: Detailed imaging parameters are summarized in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Table 1.
Imaging parameters for the CS and GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-TOF Parameters CS-3D-TOF (Sequence No.
20) GRAPPA-3D-TOF (Sequence No.

19) TE/TR (ms) 7,15 / 23,3 7,15 / 23,3 FA (Flip Angle) 20 o 20 o FOV (Frequency x Phase) (mm) 220 x 197 220 × 197 Nominal Resolution (mm) 0.73 x 0.72 x 0.78 0.82 x 0.81 x 0.99 Scan length (Z-axis) (mm) 81,6 81,6 Number of 3D blocks 4 4 Number of Slices 136 136 Interpolation 1,5 1,5 Slice Thickness (mm) 0.6 0.6 Matrix (Frequency x Phase) 304 x 269 272 x 242 Bandwidth (Hz/Pixel) 100 100 Acceleration factor 7 (CS factor) 2 (GRAPPA factor) Denoising auto N/A Scan time (min:sec) 3:04 5:00 IMAGE ANALYSIS All 3D-TOF datasets where pseudonymized, randomized, and independently assessed by two blinded readers (7 (CGI) and 14 years' (BS) neuroradiology experience).
Readers were blinded to sequence identity, but aneurysm number and location were provided in advance for each patient.
Each patient was analyzed only once per session, with either CS-accelerated or GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-TOF.

Subjective image quality parameters were rated on a 100point scale (0 = poor (insufficient for diagnosis / severe artifacts),50 = adequate (moderate artifacts not impairing diagnosis),100 = excellent (no artifacts)) across predefined criteria (see endpoints).
CNR was calculated for each TOF acquisition using predefined ROIs in the aneurysm lumen, brain stem and background noise.
Aneurysm diameters were measured in a standardized manner and recorded numerically in millimeters (mm) (see supplementary material).
Mean and maximum diameters were calculated.
As temporally matched DSA as reference standard was unavailable for most patients, neither diagnostic detection accuracy nor measurement accuracy relative to ground truth were assessed.
Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS Version 30 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA) and SAS ® Analytics Software (Online Studio) (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA).
Standard descriptive statistics were applied.
Non-inferiority of CS relative to GRAPPA for the primary endpoint (overall image quality) was assessed separately for each rater using log-transformed scores.
This was done using a one-sided t-test with a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 10%, a difference considered clinically acceptable for overall diagnostic performance (23).

Non-inferiority was concluded if the lower bound of the one-sided 95% CI for the mean difference (CS -GRAPPA) exceeded the predefined margin.
The threshold for significance was set at a p < 0.05.

Visual comparisons of secondary endpoints were performed using split-violin plots to explore potential determinants of the main result (primary endpoint).

Interrater agreements between rater A and rater B for CS and GRAPPA for all endpoints were reported as single-measures intraclass correlation coefficients derived from a two-way mixed-effects model with absolute agreement.

text.text: Across these parameters, ratings demonstrated considerable interrater variability, with generally low to moderate interrater agreement.
For several measures, Rater B tended to assign higher scores to CS-accelerated images, whereas Rater A more frequently favored GRAPPAaccelerated images.
Median scores for most secondary endpoints were broadly comparable between acceleration methods, and no consistent pattern of superiority was observed across raters.

Objective contrast-to-noise ratio, obtained through ROI-based measurements, was higher for GRAPPA than for CS, with a median of 278.2 (IQR 181.0-366.2) compared with 169.6 (IQR 91.0-226.9), respectively (Figure 3).

In contrast to the low interrater agreement observed for subjective image quality assessments, these findings indicate that objective morphometric measurements are robust and reproducible and are largely unaffected by rater preference or acceleration technique. = antero-posterior; LL = latero-lateral; CC = cranio-caudal..
3D-TOF-MRA is an established method for evaluating intracranial aneurysms, offering high diagnostic performance without exposure to ionizing radiation or contrast agents (24).
text.formatted: 3D-TOF-MRA is an established method for evaluating intracranial aneurysms, offering high diagnostic performance without exposure to ionizing radiation or contrast agents <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref>.

text.text: However, long acquisition times, limited spatial resolution, and flow-related signal loss limit its clinical applicability.
Acceleration strategies aim to shorten scan time and/or improve spatial resolution.
PI techniques (GRAPPA, CAIPIRINHA) reduce acquisition time but incur SNR penalties at higher acceleration factors (5, 8).
text.formatted: PI techniques (GRAPPA, CAIPIRINHA) reduce acquisition time but incur SNR penalties at higher acceleration factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, CS enables higher acceleration through incoherent k-space undersampling combined with iterative reconstruction (10, 11).
text.formatted: In contrast, CS enables higher acceleration through incoherent k-space undersampling combined with iterative reconstruction <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11)</ref>.

text.text: TOF-MRA is particularly well suited to CS due to sparse vessel signal against a suppressed background.

In aneurysm focused studies, pretherapeutic 3T data indicates that CS-TOF is a suitable alternative, providing similar or superior image quality and diagnostic performance to PI-TOF, with equivalent aneurysm size measurements when validated against DSA (22, 25).
text.formatted: In aneurysm focused studies, pretherapeutic 3T data indicates that CS-TOF is a suitable alternative, providing similar or superior image quality and diagnostic performance to PI-TOF, with equivalent aneurysm size measurements when validated against DSA <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, CS-TOF offers equal or improved parent vessel visualization in coiled aneurysms (26).  known to be shaped by perceptual and cognitive factors, potentially accounting for limited interobserver agreement even in technically standardized datasets and indicating readerspecific weighting of features rather than systematic inferiority of either technique (27).

text.text: While these discrepancies were isolated, they might have disproportionately affected ratings and contributed to variability.
Outlier analyses further outline the sensitivity of subjective scoring to detection variability, as a few aneurysms showed discordant detection between techniques and readers.

For instance, a single missed aneurysm affected multiple subjective metrics in Rater A, while in Rater B, a different aneurysm was not identified on CS but was detected on GRAPPA, and one additional aneurysm was identified exclusively on GRAPPA images.

Similarly, a submillimetric MCA aneurysm was not visualized by either reader on either sequence, whereas a 3.4 mm extradural ICA aneurysm and a 1.6 mm anterior choroidal aneurysm were detected on GRAPPA but not CS-accelerated 3D-TOF by one reader.
Although these discrepancies were isolated, they might have disproportionately affected ratings and contributed to variability.

Aside from reader variability, these findings may also suggest reduced conspicuity of very small aneurysms when applying CS-acceleration, although the small number of discordant cases precludes definitive conclusions regarding differences in diagnostic sensitivity.
Quantitative measurements showed substantially lower CNR for CS than GRAPPA (CS median 169.6, IQR 91.0-226.9; GRAPPA median 278.2, IQR 181.0-366.2).

This contrasts with several 3T reports where CS-TOF yielded higher CNR than PI-based accelerations, likely reflecting field-strength dependency: higher baseline SNR at 3T may allow CS to suppress noise while preserving signal, whereas 1.5T's lower baseline signal may lead to disproportionate signal attenuation and reduced CNR (22, 28).

text.text: Limitations include the lack of temporally matched DSA as a reference standard for most patients and the fact that readers were informed of the number and location of the aneurysms, precluding definitive assessment of diagnostic accuracy relative to ground truth.
Accordingly, this study assessed equivalence rather than establish true sensitivity or specificity.
Second, the opposing reader preferences and low interrater agreement slightly limit robustness and generalizability of the subjective non-inferiority conclusion.

Third, the cohort was predominantly composed of small aneurysms (65.6% < 5 mm), thus limiting generalizability, particularly given evidence that 3D TOF-MRA has reduced sensitivity for aneurysms under 3 mm, may be affected by slow or turbulent flow in large or giant aneurysms and given our observation of reduced conspicuity in isolated very small aneurysms (30).

text.text: Prior studies have suggested that PI may be preferred in the latter, potentially due to turbulence-related signal loss inherent to CS techniques (22).
text.formatted: Prior studies have suggested that PI may be preferred in the latter, potentially due to turbulence-related signal loss inherent to CS techniques <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref>.

text.text: Further work is needed in complex morphologies and very small or larger aneurysms.
Most aneurysms were in the anterior circulation and intradural, which limits extrapolation to posterior or extradural locations.
Fourth, the optimized CS and GRAPPA protocols slightly differed in matrix and nominal spatial resolution.
However, even at identical nominal resolution, a direct comparison would remain limited, as CS undersampling can reduce effective resolution despite higher nominal values.
Practically, CS provided a substantial acquisition-time reduction (38.7%) compared to GRAPPA.
This aligns with prior reports, although acceleration gains vary with field strength and implemented acceleration factors (22, 26, 28).
text.formatted: This aligns with prior reports, although acceleration gains vary with field strength and implemented acceleration factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28)</ref>.

text.text: We used a relatively high acceleration factor (7) at 1.5T, which, despite maintaining non-inferior overall image quality coincided with a substantially reduced CNR and divergent reader preferences, suggesting that choice of acceleration factor may be limited at lower field strengths.

Against the background of prior 3T studies, where CS acceleration generally benefited from higher intrinsic CNR, our findings indicate that the balance between acceleration, image quality, and perceptual consistency may be more constrained at 1.5T.
At 1.5 T, the optimized CS-accelerated 3D-TOF sequence reduced acquisition time by 38.7% and met the prespecified 10% non-inferiority margin for overall image quality for both raters.
However, opposing preferences, low interrater agreement and substantially lower ROI-based CNR demonstrate and important protocol trade-off.
Aneurysm diameter measurements were highly reproducible between readers with both techniques.

CS-accelerated 3D TOF-MRA at 1.5T is therefore as a time-efficient alternative to GRAPPA for evaluation of known intracranial aneurysms, although caution is warranted in very small aneurysms intracranial aneurysms, highlighting the need for further studies on field-strength dependency and optimal acceleration strategies.

The individualized MRI protocol included the two preselected, optimized CS-and GRAPPAaccelerated TOF-MRA sequences in addition to clinically indicated sequences.

AP
Against this background, we prospectively compared two independently optimized CS-and GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-TOF-MRA sequences at 1.5T in patients with known untreated intracranial aneurysms.
This extends existing evidence to a widely used clinical field strength in a controlled prospective setting.
In contrast to prior literature, our findings demonstrated marked heterogeneity in reader preference for CS-TOF versus GRAPPA-TOF, an observation limited however by the small number of readers (n=2).
By contrast, Kim et al. reported a clear consensus favoring CS-TOF (p < 0.001), with substantial interobserver agreement (κ = 0.78-0.81) (22).
text.formatted: By contrast, Kim et al. reported a clear consensus favoring CS-TOF (p < 0.001), with substantial interobserver agreement (κ = 0.78-0.81) (22).

text.text: Although each reader separately met the prespecified non-inferiority criterion, Rater A preferred GRAPPA (mean difference -0.062), whereas Rater B favored CS (mean difference 0.059), yielding low interrater agreement (ICC = 0.241-0.262) and opposite directional preferences.

Potential explanations include field-strength-related image texture differences and the use of a 100point continuous rating scale, which may detect subtle, reader-specific preferences not captured by coarser ordinal scales used in prior work.
This heterogeneity extended to exploratory secondary endpoints.

Rater A consistently preferred GRAPPA across all evaluated parameters, while Rater B favored CS for overall image quality, general artifact burden, and aneurysm depiction, yet preferring GRAPPA for motion artifacts, subjective CNR, and aneurysm delineation.
Subjective interpretation is

ROI-based CNR comparisons between CS and GRAPPA are not straightforward due to distinct noise behaviours: CS uses incoherent undersampling with nonlinear iterative reconstruction, whereas GRAPPA relies on coil sensitivity information and is subject to spatially varying noise amplification (geometry factor).

Moreover, CNR also depends on voxel size, nominal resolution, matrix and bandwidth, so lower CNR in CS-TOF should be interpreted cautiously as a sequence-specific trade-off rather than inherent inferiority(29).
